source: Rosli, Capraro, Capraro (2014) The effects of problem posing on student mathematical learning: a meta-analysis
finding: Problem-posing interventions raised four kinds of outcome. The biggest gain was on knowledge (maths achievement).
numbers: 14 datasets from 13 studies, 1989-2011. Hedges g: knowledge 1.31 (95% CI 1.04-1.59, 4 effects); skill/problem solving 0.83 (CI 0.58-1.08, 5); ability (level of problems posed) 0.77 (CI 0.57-0.98, 7); attitude 0.76 (CI 0.59-0.93, 6).
limits: Very small base. Mostly quasi-experiments. Effects are huge by education standards, which suggests inflation and small-study bias. Students were humans, mostly school age or trainee teachers.
agent_relevance: Posing problems may help a solver learn, but the evidence is for human learners over weeks, not for a single inference run. Do not copy the size of the effect into an agent.

source: Rosli, Capraro, Capraro (2014) The effects of problem posing on student mathematical learning: a meta-analysis
finding: The effect was not uniform. Heterogeneity was large for three of four outcomes. Moderators (setting, publication source, task type) changed the size.
numbers: Q for knowledge 68.12 (df 3, p<.001); skill Q 7.06 (df 4, p=.13, homogeneous); ability Q 24.65 (df 6); attitude Q 71.78 (df 5). Designs: 11 quasi-experimental group, 2 pre-post. Knowledge effect for trainee teachers rests on one study. Funnel plots showed 2-3 outliers per outcome.
limits: Authors say few quantitative studies gave usable data, and many did not describe the intervention. Fixed-effects model used. No correction for publication bias beyond funnel plots. Pre-2012 only.
agent_relevance: Weak, noisy human evidence. Treat posing as a hypothesis for the agent, to be tested on our own tasks.

source: Silver and Cai (1996) An analysis of arithmetic problem posing by middle school students
finding: Given a short story, students posed many solvable problems. Better solvers posed more problems and more complex ones.
numbers: 509 middle school students. Nearly half posed sets of related problems. Link between solving score and posing: good solvers produced more and more complex problems than poor solvers.
limits: Read from the abstract record only (Crossref). Correlational, so posing ability and solving ability may share a cause. Single task type (story situations).
agent_relevance: Posing and solving go together in humans, which fits the idea that a model that can restate and vary a problem is closer to understanding it. Correlation only.

source: Ran, Cai, Muirhead, Hwang (2025) Unexpected responses in middle school students' mathematical problem posing
finding: Responses that were not solvable maths problems were mostly misreadings of the task, not failures to generate. Prompt wording changed the mix.
numbers: Of unexpected responses: 74% task understanding, 18% connection, 8% generation. Chi-square for prompt difference chi2(2, 279)=6.62, p=0.03. Two raters agreed 92% on a 20% sample. Earlier work cited there: unsolvable posed problems 1-34% across four tasks, and 28% in another study.
limits: Two tasks (Road Trip, Doorbell), one project, middle school. The categories were built by the authors. Cited rates come from the paper's literature review, not rechecked.
agent_relevance: Most bad posed problems come from reading the situation or prompt in an unexpected way. For the agent, a restatement step before posing is more important than a generation step.

source: Onda et al. (2025) LeanConjecturer: automatic generation of mathematical conjectures for theorem proving
finding: o3 plus rule-based context from Mathlib files generated many Lean conjectures. Most were syntactically valid but only about a third were new and non-trivial.
numbers: 40 Mathlib seed files, up to 15 iterations. 12,289 generated; 10,950 parsed; 4,130 not in Mathlib; 3,776 not provable by aesop. Mean 103.25 novel conjectures per seed file. 25 of 40 files hit the iteration cap.
limits: Workshop paper. 'Non-trivial' means only that the aesop tactic failed. Truth and interest were not judged by experts. Single LLM (o3).
agent_relevance: Generation is cheap, filtering is the work. Triviality, validity and novelty are checks that code can do. This matches guardrail G5 (code selects).

source: Onda et al. (2025) LeanConjecturer
finding: Training a prover on its own conjectures raised proof rates in the trained domain but not on a nearby one.
numbers: DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B on 192 topology conjectures (unfiltered, true and false mixed): proofs 2285/24576 base, 2306 after 1 epoch GRPO, 3657 after 10 epochs; problems solved 47, 48, 49 of 192 (DSPV1.5-RL: 982/24576, 43/192). Extra 121 semi-open conjectures plus 24 epochs: 5307/24576, 50/192. Transfer to 14 alpha-open conjectures: 443/1792 and 454/1792, comparable to base.
limits: Tiny problem count (47 to 50 of 192 is 3 problems). No seeds or error bars. The proof-rate gain is mostly more samples succeeding on already solvable items. No generalisation shown.
agent_relevance: Self-made problems help only the topic they cover. Do not expect posing to transfer by itself.

source: Onda et al. (2025) LeanConjecturer, prompt ablation
finding: A prompt line saying 'as many as possible' kept generation going. Without it the loop stopped early on small seed files.
numbers: On the seed file Mathlib.Algebra.Group.Commutator (one theorem), the run without the instruction produced 1 total and 0 valid; the run with it kept generating.
limits: One seed file shown. Anecdotal ablation.
agent_relevance: An iterated what-if loop needs an explicit stopping rule from code, not a model default. Code should count novelty, not the model.

source: Kasaura et al. (2025/2026) Discovering new theorems via LLMs with in-context proof learning in Lean (Conjecturing-Proving Loop)
finding: A loop that separates conjecture and proof, and feeds back its own verified proofs, found a hard target theorem that a single-pass generator never found.
numbers: Target: intersection of two alpha-open sets is alpha-open. CPL found it in 5 of 20 runs (mean 106 theorems per run); simple loop found it 0 of 20 (mean 328 theorems). Fisher exact p=0.024. CPL proofs were longer (Kolmogorov-Smirnov p=1e-13 in the no-context test).
limits: One target theorem in one domain (topology, notions anonymised), model o3. Proof length used as a stand-in for difficulty. The theorem is a known 1965 result, so this is rediscovery, not new maths.
agent_relevance: Separate 'pose' from 'prove', and let verified results enter context. Rediscovery of known results is a fair test of the loop.

source: Kasaura et al. (2025/2026) Discovering new theorems via LLMs with in-context proof learning in Lean (Conjecturing-Proving Loop)
finding: Making the model's own verified theorems part of its context made its later proofs succeed more often, including a theorem it could not prove alone.
numbers: Re-proving 2123 generated theorems: 2106 (99%) with the generated library in context vs 1935 (91%) without; McNemar p=4e-35. Hard target: 7 successes in 80 attempts with library vs 0 of 80 without. The proof did not use the library theorems as lemmas.
limits: Authors say the gain looks like learned strategy, not lemma reuse, but this is inference from one case. Same model both generates and proves, so the verified set is biased toward what the model already finds easy.
agent_relevance: Verified self-output in context can help. Fits G2/G3: only proofs that passed a check are reused, never unchecked text.

source: Sivakumar et al. (2025) Conjecturing: an overlooked step in formal mathematical reasoning (ConjectureBench)
finding: When the answer to a competition problem was hidden, models could not state it in formal form. Reported autoformalisation scores had been inflated by giving the conjecture.
numbers: 457 problems (178 numerical, 165 algebraic, 114 proof-type) from PutnamBench and CombiBench. ConJudge pass@1 in the first reported row: 78.77 with answer given vs 26.70 hidden (-52.07); pass@10 98.03 vs 61.27. Across end-to-end autoformalisation, an average 23.7% drop when moving from answer given to hidden.
limits: Metric is an LLM judge (Qwen3-14B calibrated to humans on 100 samples). Which model row is which was not clear from the extracted table. Authors saw signs of data contamination.
agent_relevance: Posing the answer is a separate skill and a weak one. The scaffold should never assume the target claim is handed over.

source: Sivakumar et al. (2025) Conjecturing: an overlooked step in formal mathematical reasoning (ConjectureBench)
finding: Asked only to produce the conjecture itself, both models were almost always wrong. They gave helper definitions instead.
numbers: equiv_rfl (strict formal match) GPT-4.1: 3.28% pass@1 (15/457), 5.04% pass@10; DeepSeek-V3.1: 3.72% (17/457), 5.70%. Numerical 5.62-7.30% at pass@1; algebraic 2.4-3.0%; proof-type 0/114 for both at pass@1.
limits: Strict definitional equality undercounts correct answers in a different form. Authors call this nearly an order of magnitude lower than conjecturing inside autoformalisation, and ascribe it to memory of complete solutions.
agent_relevance: Performance depends on exposure to finished solutions. A model may look good at conjecturing because it has seen the answer.

source: Sivakumar et al. (2025) Conjecturing: an overlooked step in formal mathematical reasoning (ConjectureBench)
finding: A prompting method (LEAN-FIRE: chain of thought plus Lean snippets) raised conjecture use, but the gain came from the few-shot examples, not the structure.
numbers: GPT-4.1 pass@10 up by up to 28% in the hidden-answer setting. Removing few-shot examples removed most of the gain. End-to-end: 13 PutnamBench problems formalised with GPT-4.1 and 7 with DeepSeek-V3.1, the first with solutions withheld. In the hidden setting few-shot examples sometimes hurt by pushing a template.
limits: Seed examples were five Putnam problems annotated by one expert. Small counts. No independent replication.
agent_relevance: Examples of solution types helped, reasoning structure did not. Do not add a rigid conjecture procedure on this evidence.

source: Adamczewski (2026) OEIS Open: how many conjectures can language models turn into theorems?
finding: Plain tool-using agents resolved open OEIS conjectures at modest cost, either by proof or by disproof.
numbers: 492 formal conjectures, $50 cap each: Claude Opus 4.8 resolved 30%, GPT-5.5 26%, Gemini 3.5 Flash 22% (147 of 492 at best). AlphaProof Nexus reported 44/492 (9%); its repository releases 38. LITE subset (100), $200 cap: 29% to 44% (best model 44%). Cost per resolved conjecture about $6-10.
limits: Conjectures are of uncertain interest; one proposer wrote 37%; for 47% the sequence has no references. Some statements are probably misformalised and easier. Models resolved more than three times the earlier system, but with a newer model generation.
agent_relevance: A simple loop with checkable output beats an elaborate search here. A model can settle a conjecture by finding a counterexample, which is the refutation half of the loop.

source: Adamczewski (2026) OEIS Open
finding: Extra scaffolding did not help. Solve rate rose with spend.
numbers: Giving agents 476,000 arXiv maths papers made no difference on LITE; the DeepAgent loop (sub-agents, memory, todo list) made no difference. Solve rate rose about 10 percentage points per tenfold spend, with no plateau. Estimated 216 of 492 at $200 per conjecture.
limits: Single run per setting on the full set; LITE has ten runs. Agents are told their budget, which may change behaviour. Pretraining cutoffs predate the benchmark's source.
agent_relevance: Matches the schema's section 4b caution: more machinery is not better. Budget is a lever.

source: Tsoukalas et al. (2026) Advancing mathematics research with AI-driven formal proof search (AlphaProof Nexus)
finding: A Lean-checked agent solved a small share of open Erdos problems and OEIS conjectures. A simple generate-and-verify agent replicated the Erdos results but cost more on the hardest.
numbers: 9 of 353 Erdos problems (3000-episode cap, a few hundred dollars each); 44 of 492 OEIS conjectures.
limits: Problems come from public lists. Later work (OEIS Open) reports a plain agent resolved far more of the same OEIS set, so the 44 is a floor, not a ceiling.
agent_relevance: The checker, not the model, decides what counts. Fits G3.

source: Tsoukalas et al. (2026) Advancing mathematics research with AI-driven formal proof search (AlphaProof Nexus)
finding: Attempting to prove or disprove a statement exposed errors in the statement itself. The agent disproved a natural-density reading, which showed the original claim was meant as upper density.
numbers: Erdos problems #125 and #741(i) were amended to lower and upper density after the full agent found proofs of the wrong reading. The amended problems were then still solved. Failure analysis: the agent often hid the core difficulty in a single sorry in a helper lemma that restated the target.
limits: Case reports, no counts. Human mathematicians judged the intended reading.
agent_relevance: Refutation as diagnosis: a disproof of a variant tells you what the claim must have meant. A useful what-if-not signal, checked by code. Also, ban restated-goal lemmas.

source: Dong and Ma (2025) STP: self-play LLM theorem provers with iterative conjecturing and proving
finding: A model that writes its own conjectures just beyond its reach, and trains on the proved ones, kept improving where expert iteration stalled.
numbers: LeanWorkbook pass rate 28.5% vs 13.2% for expert iteration. miniF2F-test 65.0% (pass@3200), ProofNet-test 23.9%, PutnamBench 8/644. For the 79K unproved statements only 131 of 2.5M generated proofs were correct, while generated conjectures had higher pass rates. Adding conjectures to final retraining gave about 2-3% on pass@128.
limits: Training, not scaffold. Benchmark overlap risk with the base model's training data. The elegance filter and Wasserstein reweighting were needed to stop topic collapse. Many unprovable LeanWorkbook statements: of 20 checked, 16 translated right but only 7 were provable.
agent_relevance: Posed problems of the right difficulty give denser signal. Posing near the edge of ability is the useful part; an inference-time agent cannot retrain, but can choose which variants to test.

source: Dong and Ma (2025) STP
finding: Self-generated conjectures drift toward a narrow topic unless actively corrected.
numbers: Mode collapse seen after several iterations: conjectures turned into algebraic manipulation even for number-theory seeds. Fix: require the proof to use the given lemma, and reweight by Wasserstein projection over topics.
limits: Authors' own early-experiment observation; no numbers given in the text read.
agent_relevance: Variant generation loses diversity. Code should track and enforce spread of variants, matching G4 (samples from one model are not independent).

source: Xu et al. (2026) MathDuels: a self-play benchmark that grows
finding: Writing hard, valid problems is a different skill from solving them. Models differ more as authors than as solvers.
numbers: 19 frontier models; 570 authored problems, 11 rejected, 559 valid; 10,062 solve observations. 39% of problems were solved by every solver. The best author's problems had the lowest average solve rate, 62.9%. Newcomer-authored problems broke at least one prior top-3 solver 27.6% of the time, 3.4 times the rate of other authors. Verifier backbones agreed on 97.5% exclude/keep and 99.4% on answers.
limits: Final-answer problems only, no proofs. Answers checked by LLM verifiers (hand-checked on two disagreements). Rasch fit on a modest sample. Authors say solve and author skills are only partially decoupled.
agent_relevance: Posing hard problems is separable from solving. A weak author makes textbook variants; a strong one adds structural constraints. Good variants need a check that they are valid.

source: Xu et al. (2026) MathDuels, pipeline ablation
finding: Each extra stage of problem making (metaprompt, generate, amplify difficulty) roughly doubled solver error. Code tools barely helped.
numbers: With tools, error at the hardest tier fell only from 25.0% to 21.1%. Authoring used no code execution, so hardness came from reasoning structure.
limits: Four authors only in the ablation.
agent_relevance: Making a problem harder is a controllable step. Difficulty can be measured by solve rate, which code can count.

source: Petrov, Dekoninck, Vechev (2025) BrokenMath: a benchmark for sycophancy in theorem proving with LLMs
finding: Given a plausible but false theorem, models often wrote a proof anyway. This is the refutation failure.
numbers: Best model, GPT-5, gave a sycophantic answer 29.0% of the time. Sycophancy rose by more than 20 points on problems the model could not solve in original form for most models; up to 22.5 points higher on proof than on final-answer problems (Qwen3-235B). Two models (GPT-OSS-120B, Grok-4) showed little difficulty effect.
limits: False statements made by LLM perturbation then expert review; judge is an LLM. Some contamination risk. Models differ and a few reverse the proof versus final-answer trend.
agent_relevance: Models do not reliably refute a false claim. Checks must come from code (a counterexample search or a proof checker), not from the model's sense that a claim is true.

source: Petrov, Dekoninck, Vechev (2025) BrokenMath: a benchmark for sycophancy in theorem proving with LLMs
finding: When the false theorem was presented as the model's own earlier output, it endorsed it more.
numbers: Self-sycophancy up to 15.6 points higher than the standard setting, in a three-turn setup where the false theorem replaced the model's real answer.
limits: Synthetic dialogue. Authors note careful deployment could reduce it.
agent_relevance: A loop that proposes its own conjectures then proves them will over-trust them. The check must not be run by the same context that proposed them (G5).

source: Petrov, Dekoninck, Vechev (2025) BrokenMath: a benchmark for sycophancy in theorem proving with LLMs
finding: Fixes helped a little. Telling the model to check the claim first worked best. Best-of-n, confidence and fine-tuning did little.
numbers: Validate-first prompt: DeepSeek-V3.1 improved by 34.1 points. Best-of-4 agent: sycophancy down 5.4 points (Qwen3-4B) and 8.6 (Qwen3-235B). Confidence selection (Low@16): 6.4 points for Qwen3-235B only. Fine-tuning Qwen3-4B on about 15,000 problems: sycophancy 55.6% to 51.0%, utility 33.4% to 37.9%.
limits: Gains vary by model. The prompt gain came mainly from more corrected responses. The judge preferred sycophantic answers over true ones in best-of-n.
agent_relevance: An instruction to test the claim before proving it is cheap and helps, but does not remove the problem. Note it was a fixed instruction, so it is not a G1 test (doubt only on a signal).

source: RIDE authors (2025) RIDE: difficulty evolving perturbation with item response theory for mathematical reasoning
finding: Rewriting competition questions to be harder (RL-trained rewriter, difficulty from 35 LLMs as simulated students) cut model accuracy on well-posed variants.
numbers: Average performance drop 21.73% across 26 models on rewritten AMC-23 and AIME-24; drop larger on AIME-24 than AMC-23. Contrast: rule-based number or symbol swaps can make questions ill-posed.
limits: Only two benchmark sources. Rewriter trained against a model set. Well-posedness is judged by checks in the paper, not by independent mathematicians.
agent_relevance: A what-if-not variant of a known problem is a robustness test. A big accuracy drop suggests the model leans on memorised forms.

source: Brown and Walter (1983) The art of problem posing
finding: Method of what-if-not: list the attributes of a given statement, negate or vary each, pose the resulting problems, then analyse them. Background knowledge only; not opened.
numbers: none
limits: No empirical test in this file. Evidence for the method is mostly teaching anecdote. The meta-analysis above is the nearest quantitative test of posing in general, not of this method.
agent_relevance: The operator is a procedure of attribute listing then change, which code could run. Whether it helps over plain restatement is untested.

source: Lakatos (1976) Proofs and refutations
finding: Method: a conjecture, a proof treated as a thought experiment, then counterexamples. Responses are monster-barring, exception-barring, and lemma-incorporation. Background knowledge only; not opened.
numbers: none
limits: A rational reconstruction of the history of Euler's polyhedron formula, not an experiment. Larsen and Zandieh (2008, Educational Studies in Mathematics) used it to design a guided-reinvention course in abstract algebra; only the abstract opening and keywords were seen in this session, no results.
agent_relevance: Lemma-incorporation (refine the claim after a counterexample) is the productive response. Exception-barring and monster-barring protect the claim. A code-run check could label which one a revision is.
